subtitulo: Putting the weight where you want it in everyday talk
descripcion: English word order is rigid, so shifting emphasis requires structural moves rather than the free reordering Spanish allows. These structures are the clearest single marker separating C1 writing from B2 writing, and the most reliably absent from advanced learners' output.

filas: *Not until / Only after / Rarely / Never / Little* + **aux + subject**
Not until I'd lived there did I understand.
What struck me was the silence.
It was the bureaucracy that broke me.
*All I wanted was…* / *The thing that got me was…*

ejemplos.texto: *Not until I'd lived there a year did I understand why nobody complains.*
*What struck me most wasn't the language — it was the silence on trains.*
*It was the bureaucracy, not the weather, that nearly broke me.*
*All I wanted was somebody to explain the recycling.*
*Little did I know how long the paperwork would take.*

notas: Negative inversion requires auxiliary inversion: *Not only did I…*, never *Not only I did…*.
These structures are marked. Two or three in a text is stylish; six is theatrical.
The *All I wanted was* pattern is the one to start with: informal, frequent, and it teaches the cleft logic without the formal register.

es.en: Spanish moves emphasis by moving words («a mí no me gustó»). English cannot, so it builds a structure instead. Every Spanish emphatic word-order shift needs a cleft or an inversion in English, not a word-order change.
es.es: El español desplaza el énfasis moviendo palabras («a mí no me gustó»). El inglés no puede hacerlo de esa manera, por lo que construye una estructura. Cada cambio enfático de orden en español necesita en inglés un «cleft» o una inversión, no simplemente otro orden de palabras.

de.en: Because German is verb-second, negative openers are followed by inversion automatically («Nie habe ich so etwas gesehen»), which makes Never have I seen… feel natural. The difficulty is do-support: Never thought I is a typical calque of «Nie dachte ich». It-clefts are used less in German, so they need deliberate practice.
de.de: Weil Deutsch Verbzweitstellung hat, folgt auf negative Satzanfänge automatisch Inversion («Nie habe ich so etwas gesehen»), wodurch «Never have I seen…» natürlich wirkt. Die Schwierigkeit ist «do-support»: «Never thought I» ist eine typische Übertragung von «Nie dachte ich». «It-clefts» sind im Deutschen weniger üblich und müssen bewusst geübt werden.

it.en: Italian can focus the subject simply by placing it after the verb («L'ha detto Maria»), where English needs a cleft (It was Maria who said it). Italian speakers therefore need clefts more often than they expect; negative inversion with do-support has no Italian model.
it.it: L'italiano può mettere a fuoco il soggetto semplicemente collocandolo dopo il verbo («L'ha detto Maria»), dove l'inglese richiede un «cleft» («It was Maria who said it»). Gli italofoni devono quindi usare i «cleft» più spesso di quanto si aspettino; la «negative inversion» con «do-support» non ha un modello italiano.

fr.en: It-clefts are the default emphasis in French («c'est… qui/que»), so they come very easily, sometimes too often. Literary French also inverts after openers such as «rarement» or «à peine» («Rarement a-t-on vu…»), a close model for Rarely have we seen….
fr.fr: Les «it-clefts» sont le procédé d'emphase par défaut en français («c'est… qui/que»), donc ils viennent très facilement, parfois trop. Le français littéraire inverse aussi après des amorces comme «rarement» ou «à peine» («Rarement a-t-on vu…»), excellent modèle pour «Rarely have we seen…».

pt.en: Portuguese focuses through free word order and clefts («foi a Maria que disse»), so it-clefts come easily. The pseudo-cleft is especially frequent («o que eu quero é…»), which makes what I want is… natural; negative inversion has no Portuguese model.
pt.pt: O português cria foco com ordem livre e «clefts» («foi a Maria que disse»), então «it-clefts» vêm com facilidade. A «pseudo-cleft» é especialmente frequente («o que eu quero é…»), o que torna «what I want is…» natural; «negative inversion» não tem modelo em português.

errores: *Never I have seen* instead of *Never have I seen*.
Using inversion where plain order carries the same weight, so the emphasis reads as unearned.

es: «*fue entonces cuando*» rendered as *It was then when…* instead of *It was then that…*.
de: Inverting after any fronted adverb, as German V2 requires: *Then have I realised* instead of *Then I realised*.
it: Dropping the dummy subject in a cleft, as in «*è Maria che ha deciso*»: *Is Maria who decided* instead of *It was Maria who decided*.
fr: Using *it is … that* for every emphasis because «*c'est … que*» is the default French focus device, producing clefts where stress alone would do.
pt: Dropping the dummy subject in a cleft, as in «*é a Maria que decidiu*»: *Is Maria who decided* instead of *It was Maria who decided*.

traducciones.pt: Só depois de… é que eu…

traducciones.it: Ciò che mi ha colpito è stato…
traducciones.pt: O que me chamou a atenção foi…

traducciones.fr: Tout ce que je voulais, c’était…
traducciones.pt: Tudo o que eu queria era…

redemittel.expresion: The thing that got me was…

traducciones.fr: Ce qui m’a le plus marqué, c’est…
traducciones.it: La cosa che mi ha colpito è stata…
traducciones.pt: O que me apanhou de surpresa foi…

traducciones.fr: J’étais loin de me douter que…

mision.consigna: Describe your real kitchen habits to someone who thinks you cook more than you do.
requisitos: one negative inversion (*Rarely do I…*, *Not until… did I…*)
use *leftovers*, *a go-to recipe* and *to throw something together*

microtareas.texto: Write your *go-to recipe* in three sentences, then rewrite the last one as a *what*-cleft.
Five sentences starting with *Rarely*, *Never*, *Only when*, *Not until*, *Little did I*. All about food.
Record 90 seconds: are you a *fussy eater* or do you have a *sweet tooth*? Two clefts minimum.

autochequeo: Is the auxiliary present in every inversion?
Two different cleft types, or the same one twice?
Does each one earn its emphasis, or is it decoration?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on inversion, clefts and emphatic structures. (1) Check the auxiliary in every inversion. (2) Say whether each structure earns its emphasis or is decorative. (3) Show where plain word order would be better. (4) Give one alternative structure for my three best sentences. Do not rewrite the text.
